3950:
When you call someone debonair, you are saying they are a special combination of three things at once: charming, confident, and effortlessly stylish. The key word here is effortlessly. A debonair person doesn't seem to be trying to be impressive — they simply are, naturally and without any visible effort.

Think of it this way: if confidence is wearing a fine suit, and charm is smiling warmly at everyone in the room, then being debonair is doing both of those things while also making it look like the easiest thing in the world.
Breaking Down What Debonair Really Means

Because debonair is a layered word, it helps to look at each quality it carries:

1. Confident, but not arrogant.
A debonair person walks into a room and feels completely at ease. They are sure of themselves, but they don't show off or look down on others. Their confidence is quiet and relaxed, not loud or pushy.

2. Charming and pleasant.
They have a way of making people around them feel good. Their words are smooth, their manner is warm, and their smile feels genuine. People are naturally drawn to them.

3. Stylish and well-groomed.
Their appearance is polished and put-together — not in an overdone or flashy way, but in a clean, elegant, tasteful way. Every detail about how they present themselves feels just right.

4. Carefree and light.
There is a certain lightness to a debonair person. They don't seem stressed, worried, or awkward. Life appears to flow easily for them, and they carry themselves with a kind of breezy, relaxed grace.

5. Sophisticated and worldly.
A debonair person gives the impression that they are cultured and experienced. They seem like someone who has seen the world, knows how to behave in any situation, and handles everything with coolness and grace.

If you want one image to lock this word in your memory forever, think of the classic Hollywood actor Cary Grant, or the fictional spy James Bond. These are the poster examples of debonair. Imagine a well-dressed man who:

  • Walks into a fancy party with total ease
  • Greets everyone with a warm, confident smile
  • Says exactly the right thing without hesitating
  • Looks immaculate without appearing to have tried
  • Makes everyone in the room feel a little more impressed

That is debonair.
Who Does This Word Usually Describe?

Debonair is almost always used to describe men. It is a very masculine word in its common usage. While it's not grammatically wrong to use it for a woman, it would sound unusual to most readers and listeners. If you see it applied to a woman, it's typically either poetic, or the writer is making a deliberate stylistic choice.

It is also most naturally used to describe a person's overall manner and appearance together — not just one or the other. A man can be stylish but rude, or charming but sloppy. Debonair requires the whole package.

It's important to know what this word doesn't include, so you don't overuse or misuse it:

  • It does not mean arrogant or cocky — debonair has warmth in it.
  • It does not just mean handsome — looks alone don't make someone debonair.
  • It does not mean flashy or showy — debonair is elegant and understated, not loud.
  • It does not imply manipulation or fakeness — the charm of a debonair person feels genuine and pleasant, not suspicious.

Here are some sentences showing how the word is naturally used:

  • He strolled into the gala in a perfectly fitted tuxedo, greeted everyone by name, and charmed every person in the room — utterly debonair.
  • There was something debonair about the way he handled the awkward situation: calm, smooth, and with a slight smile.
  • She had always been attracted to his debonair manner — the easy confidence, the wit, the quiet elegance.
  • The new professor had a debonair quality that made even his most difficult lectures feel engaging and effortless.

Debonair is a positive, admiring word. When you call someone debonair, you are paying them a genuine compliment. There is no sarcasm built into it, and it carries no negative shade of meaning. It feels slightly old-fashioned and classic — like something from the golden age of cinema — which is part of what gives it its sophisticated flavour. Using it today sounds refined and deliberate.

If you had to summarize it completely:

Debonair describes a man who is naturally charming, quietly confident, polished in appearance, and graceful in manner — all without appearing to make any effort at all.
3951:
To debouch means to emerge from a narrow or confined space into a wider, open space.

Think of it like squeezing through a tight bottleneck and then suddenly spilling out into a large open area. That transition — from tight to wide, from confined to open — is the heart of what debouch means.
The Two Main Contexts Where You'll See It

This word is used most often in two areas: geography and military writing. Understanding both will cover virtually every situation where you'll ever encounter it.

1. Geography (Rivers and Terrain)

In geography, a river or stream debouches when it flows out of a narrow, confined channel — like a canyon, a gorge, or a valley — and empties into something wider and more open, like a larger river, a plain, a lake, or the sea.

"The river debouched into the open desert plain after passing through the narrow canyon."

Notice the journey: tight canyon → open desert. That's the move. The river doesn't just flow — it specifically flows from something narrow into something wide.

You might also see it used for roads or valleys:

"The mountain pass debouched onto a broad coastal plain."

Same logic. The pass is narrow and confined. The plain is wide and open. The pass debouches onto it.

2. Military (Troops Emerging from a Confined Position)

In military contexts, soldiers or an army debouch when they march out of a confined space — like a forest, a narrow pass, a ravine, or a town street — into an open area such as a battlefield or a field.

"The infantry debouched from the forest and advanced across the open ground."

This matters militarily because emerging into the open changes everything — visibility, vulnerability, tactical options. So the word doesn't just describe movement; it describes a shift in situation, from hidden and cramped to exposed and open.
What Makes It Different from Just Saying "Exit" or "Emerge"

You might wonder: why not just say "the river flowed out" or "the soldiers came out"? Here's the distinction that makes debouch its own word:

Debouch always implies a specific contrast — the thing doing the moving is coming from somewhere notably narrow or restricted, and entering somewhere notably wider or more open. It's not just about leaving a space; it's about the release from confinement into openness. That combination — confined source, open destination — is baked into the word itself.

"Exit" tells you nothing about what you're exiting into. "Debouch" tells you the full picture in one word.

The thing that debouches is almost always one of these:

  • A body of water (river, stream, glacier)
  • A group of people (troops, a crowd, passengers)
  • A road, valley, pass, or path

You would not typically say a single person debouches unless being deliberately literary or humorous. It suits flows of things — water, soldiers, masses of people, channels of terrain.

Debouch is almost always used intransitively — meaning it does not take a direct object. Things debouch into something, or they debouch on their own. You would not say "the general debouched his troops" in standard usage; you would say "the troops debouched from the pass."

This is a formal, somewhat literary word. You'll find it in:

  • Historical military accounts and war narratives
  • Geography and geology writing
  • Literary fiction, especially historical fiction
  • Academic texts

You wouldn't use it in casual everyday speech. If you use it in writing, it signals precision and a certain sophistication — you know exactly what kind of movement you're describing.

To debouch is to flow or march out of a narrow, confined space into a wider, open one — whether that's a river spilling from a canyon into the sea, or soldiers streaming out of a forest onto a battlefield.
3952:
To debrief someone means to question them carefully and systematically after they have completed a task, mission, or important event — in order to gather information about what happened, what they saw, what decisions were made, and what the results were.

The person doing the debriefing (the one asking questions) is typically someone in authority — a commander, supervisor, manager, or researcher. The person being debriefed is the one who was actually there, directly involved in what happened.

Think of it this way: the debriefed person carries valuable first-hand knowledge. The debriefer's job is to extract that knowledge in an organized, purposeful way.
The Key Feature: It Always Happens After

This is important. Debriefing always takes place after an event — never before, never during. The point is to look back at what just occurred.

This makes it the logical opposite of "brief" (verb), which means to inform or prepare someone before a task. You brief a pilot before the flight; you debrief the pilot after landing. You brief a team before the project begins; you debrief them once it's over.

So the two words form a clean pair:

  • Brief → before (giving information in advance)
  • Debrief → after (gathering information in retrospect)

The purposes are usually one or more of the following:

  • To collect information — "What exactly did you see? What happened at each stage?"
  • To identify mistakes or problems — "Where did things go wrong? Why?"
  • To capture lessons learned — "What should we do differently next time?"
  • To confirm facts — "Did the plan unfold as expected, or were there surprises?"
  • To ensure security — especially in intelligence and military work, to make sure sensitive information isn't accidentally leaked

Debriefing is used across many professional and specialized fields:

Military and intelligence: A soldier returns from a covert operation. Officers sit with that soldier and debrief them — asking point by point what they observed, who they encountered, what threats existed, and what information they gathered.

Space and aviation: After astronauts return from a mission, scientists and engineers debrief them thoroughly — asking about technical problems, physical sensations, equipment performance, and unexpected events.

Business and project management: After a major product launch or a client presentation, a manager might debrief the team — asking what went well, what failed, and what could be improved. This is one of the most common everyday uses of the word.

Medicine and emergency response: After a complex surgery or a crisis situation (like a mass casualty incident), the medical team is debriefed. This helps the hospital understand what worked, what endangered patients, and how protocols should change.

Psychology and research: This is a slightly specialized use. When researchers conduct experiments — especially ones involving deception (where participants weren't told the full truth during the study) — they are ethically required to debrief participants afterward. This means telling them the actual purpose of the study, explaining why deception was used, and ensuring participants leave without misunderstanding or harm.

Sports: After a match or training session, a coach debriefs the players — reviewing specific decisions, moments, and performances with them.

Law enforcement: After an undercover operation or a major investigation, officers are debriefed by supervisors to capture everything they observed and to create accurate records.

Notice how the verb works in different forms:

  • The general debriefed the soldiers after they returned from the mission.
    (Active: the general is asking; the soldiers are answering.)
  • The astronauts were debriefed for three days following their return to Earth.
    (Passive: focus is on the astronauts going through the process.)
  • She spent two hours debriefing the field agent about what he had witnessed.
    (The "-ing" form, showing the action in progress.)
  • He was thoroughly debriefed before being allowed to leave the building.
    (In intelligence contexts, "thoroughly debriefed" is a very common phrase.)

In modern workplaces and casual conversation, "debrief" is increasingly used without a direct object, simply to mean "let's sit down and talk through what just happened."

  • "Let's debrief after the meeting."
  • "Can we debrief before you head out?"
  • "We need to debrief on yesterday's presentation."

Here, the word is softer and more conversational — it doesn't imply a formal interrogation. It just means: let's have a structured, focused conversation about a recent event while it's still fresh.
The Noun Forms: "A Debrief" and "A Debriefing"

The word doubles as a noun in two forms:

  • A debrief — the session or meeting itself: "We have a debrief scheduled for 3 PM."
  • A debriefing — same meaning, slightly more formal: "The debriefing lasted four hours."

Both refer to the actual event — the structured conversation that takes place after the task or mission.
The Nuance That Makes It Different from an Ordinary Conversation

Debriefing is not the same as just chatting about how something went. What sets it apart:

  1. It is purposeful and structured — there are specific things the debriefer wants to know.
  2. It is comprehensive — the goal is to miss nothing important.
  3. The person being debriefed has information the other person doesn't — and the whole point is to transfer that knowledge.
  4. There's often a record kept — notes, reports, or formal documentation of what was shared.

This is why debriefing carries a slightly formal or professional tone, even in its casual everyday uses. When someone says "let's debrief," they're signaling: this isn't just small talk — I want us to think carefully and deliberately about what just happened.

To debrief someone is to question them in a thorough, organized way after a completed event, with the goal of extracting what they experienced, observed, or learned — so that knowledge isn't lost and lessons can be applied going forward.
3953:
A debriefing is a formal meeting or structured conversation that takes place after a significant event, task, mission, or experience — in which a person (or group) is carefully questioned or asked to report on what they saw, did, experienced, decided, and observed.

The purpose is to collect information, understand what happened, review performance, learn lessons, or help someone process a difficult experience.

Think of it as an "after-action review" — a deliberate, organized discussion that follows something important.
The Simplest Way to Picture It

Imagine a soldier who just returned from a dangerous mission. Before the mission, they were told what to do and what to expect — that's called a briefing. Now that they're back, a commander sits them down and asks: What did you see? What happened exactly? Did anything go wrong? What did the enemy do? Did you spot any threats? That structured session of questions and answers — that's a debriefing.

So the two words are mirror images:

  • Briefing = happens before → prepares you for what's coming
  • Debriefing = happens after → reviews what already happened
What Actually Happens in a Debriefing?

A debriefing is not a casual chat. It typically involves:

  1. Recounting the event — The person describes in detail what happened, step by step.
  2. Answering questions — Someone (often in authority) asks specific, targeted questions.
  3. Extracting key information — Important facts, observations, and data are noted down.
  4. Identifying lessons — What went right? What went wrong? What should be done differently?
  5. Processing the experience — In some cases (especially traumatic ones), a debriefing also helps a person emotionally work through what they went through.

A debriefing usually involves two sides:

  • The person being debriefed — the one who participated in the event and is now reporting back (a soldier, a spy, an astronaut, an employee, a research participant, etc.)
  • The person conducting the debriefing — someone in authority or with expertise who asks questions and gathers information (a commander, a psychologist, a manager, a researcher, etc.)

Debriefing happens across many different fields. Here's how it looks in each one:

Military & Intelligence
After a mission or covert operation, soldiers or intelligence agents are formally questioned about what they observed, who they encountered, what decisions they made, and what the outcomes were. The goal is gathering intelligence and reviewing performance.
Example: "The special forces unit underwent a three-hour debriefing following the operation."

Space Exploration
After returning from a space mission, astronauts go through extensive debriefings where scientists and mission controllers ask them about every aspect of the journey — technical problems, health observations, equipment failures, and personal experiences.
Example: "NASA scheduled a week of debriefings for the crew returning from the International Space Station."

Psychology & Trauma
After a traumatic or highly stressful event — like a natural disaster, accident, or violent incident — mental health professionals conduct a psychological debriefing to help survivors talk through what they experienced. This helps prevent long-term emotional harm and reduces stress.
Example: "Emergency responders received a psychological debriefing after dealing with the collapse."

Scientific Research
When researchers conduct experiments — especially ones involving deception (where participants weren't told the real purpose upfront) — they hold a debriefing at the end. Here, they explain the true purpose of the study, why deception was necessary, and answer any questions the participant may have. This is considered a standard ethical requirement.
Example: "After completing the study, each participant attended a debriefing where the researchers explained what the experiment was actually measuring."

Business & Corporate World
After a major project, product launch, client meeting, or business event, teams hold a debriefing to review what happened. This is also called a "post-mortem" or "retrospective" in professional settings.
Example: "The marketing team's debriefing after the campaign revealed that the social media strategy had underperformed."

Aviation
Pilots and crew are often debriefed after flights — especially training flights, emergency situations, or long-haul routes — to review their decisions and learn from the experience.

Sports & Athletics
Coaches debrief athletes after matches or competitions, reviewing gameplay, strategies, errors, and what improvements are needed.
Example: "The coach led a debriefing after the loss to analyze where the team's defense broke down."
The Key Qualities That Define a Debriefing

To make sure you never confuse debriefing with a regular conversation, remember these defining features:

  1. It is always retrospective — it looks back at something that already happened.
  2. It is structured and purposeful — not casual, but planned and goal-oriented.
  3. It involves a deliberate review — someone is specifically trying to extract information or understanding.
  4. It produces something useful — lessons, data, intelligence, emotional relief, or accountability.
  5. There is usually a clear authority or expertise involved — a commander, a psychologist, a researcher, a manager — someone who has a professional reason to conduct the session.

• The word can carry a slightly formal or even serious tone. When you say "debriefing," it implies that the event being reviewed was significant — not trivial.
  • In intelligence and military contexts, a debriefing can also serve a security function — making sure the person hasn't accidentally revealed classified information or been compromised in some way.
  • In research, debriefing is not just polite — it is an ethical obligation to participants.
  • In psychology, "debriefing" and "critical incident debriefing" are recognized therapeutic practices, not just informal chats.

• "The ambassador requested a full debriefing from the negotiating team as soon as they landed."
  • "Victims of the accident participated in a structured debriefing with a trauma counselor."
  • "The debriefing revealed several procedural errors that had contributed to the mission's failure."
  • "Standard practice required a debriefing within 24 hours of any undercover operation."
  • "The project manager scheduled a debriefing with all stakeholders to discuss what could be improved next time."

A debriefing is a formal, structured session held after a significant event in which participants are questioned, asked to report what happened, and guided to share observations — so that information can be gathered, performance assessed, lessons can be learned, or emotional experiences can be processed.
3954: Debris refers to the scattered pieces, fragments, and remnants left behind after something has been broken, destroyed, or worn down. Think of it as the "aftermath mess" — the broken bits and loose material that remain when something falls apart, collapses, or gets wrecked.
Breaking it down further

The key ideas packed into debris are:

  • Something used to be whole — but it got damaged, destroyed, or broken apart.
  • What's left behind is scattered — not neatly piled, but spread around in a disorganized way.
  • The pieces are usually useless or unwanted — they're leftovers, not the original thing anymore.
Where you'll encounter this word
Debris shows up across many real-world situations. Here are the major ones:
After a disaster or destruction

When a building collapses in an earthquake, the broken concrete, twisted metal, glass shards, and rubble scattered around are called debris. After a tornado, the planks, bricks, shattered wood, and broken objects strewn across the ground are debris. After a plane crash, the wreckage spread across the crash site is debris.
In nature

After a storm, fallen branches, torn leaves, and broken twigs covering the ground are referred to as natural debris. A rockslide leaves rocky debris at the base of a hill. Even the dead leaves, bark, and organic material on a forest floor can be called leaf debris or forest debris.
In space

Old, broken satellites, discarded rocket parts, and fragments from past space missions orbiting Earth are called space debris (or orbital debris). This is a serious real-world problem that scientists worry about.
In water
Floating pieces of broken wood, plastic, and other material drifting in a river or ocean are called debris. After a flood, the junk carried and deposited by the water is also debris.
At a construction or demolition site
When workers tear down a wall or building, the resulting pile of broken materials — chunks of concrete, bent rods, broken tiles — is called construction debris or demolition debris.
An important grammar point

Debris is an uncountable noun. This means:

  • You cannot say "a debris" or "one debris."
  • You cannot say "debries" (there is no plural form).
  • You always treat it as a singular mass: "The debris was cleared." (not "were")
  • To talk about individual pieces, you say: "a piece of debris," "chunks of debris," "a layer of debris."
The feeling the word carries

Debris always suggests disorder and destruction. It implies that something bad has happened — a collapse, a wreck, a storm, a breakdown. It is not a neutral word for "stuff lying around." It specifically signals that the material you're looking at is the disordered remains of something that once existed in a better or more complete form.

For example, the word trash or garbage refers to things you threw away intentionally. But debris refers to things that ended up scattered around because of some kind of breaking apart or destruction — not because someone chose to discard them.
Common phrases you'll see with this word

• clear the debris — to remove or clean up the scattered remains
  • sift through the debris — to carefully search through the remains (often to find survivors or clues)
  • a debris field — a wide area over which debris is spread (common in aviation crash investigations)
  • space debris — broken or discarded man-made objects orbiting Earth
  • debris flow — a geological event where a fast-moving mix of water, mud, and debris rushes down a slope (like a mudslide carrying chunks of rock and wood)
  • wreckage and debris — these two words are often paired; wreckage refers more to the identifiable remains of a specific structure (like a plane or ship), while debris is the broader scattered material
Example sentences

1. Rescue workers spent days searching through the debris of the collapsed building for survivors.
  2. The storm left a trail of debris — broken branches, roof tiles, and shattered glass — across the entire neighborhood.
  3. Scientists are working on ways to safely remove space debris from Earth's orbit before it causes collisions.
  4. After the explosion, debris was scattered across a wide area.
  5. The river carried debris downstream after the heavy rains.
  6. Investigators carefully examined each piece of debris to determine what caused the aircraft to crash.
  7. The construction crew worked all morning to haul away the debris from the demolition.
Summary in one sentence

Debris is the disordered, often broken and useless material scattered around after something — a building, a vehicle, a natural landscape, or any other thing — has been destroyed, collapsed, or broken apart.
3955:
A debt is something you owe to someone else — because they gave you something first, with the understanding (or agreement) that you will give it back or return the favour later.

The most common form of debt involves money. But debt can also involve a favour, a service, or even an emotional obligation. In all cases, the logic is the same: someone gave you something → you now owe them something in return.

When you borrow money from someone — a bank, a friend, or a company — and you haven't paid it back yet, that unpaid amount is called a debt.

"He took a loan of ₹50,000 from the bank. Until he repays it, he has a debt of ₹50,000."

The debt exists from the moment you borrow until the moment you fully repay. As long as you haven't paid it back, the debt is still there — it "hangs over" you.
The Two People in a Debt

Every debt involves exactly two sides:

  • The debtor — the person who owes money (the borrower). They are in debt.
  • The creditor — the person or institution who is owed money (the lender). They are owed the debt.

So in the bank example above, you are the debtor and the bank is the creditor.
Debt Is Not the Same as an Expense

This is a very important distinction.

When you spend money and it's gone — say, you bought a meal for ₹300 — that is an expense. You spent it, it's over, no one is waiting for repayment.

But when someone lends you ₹300 and you spend it, the money is gone but the obligation remains. You still owe ₹300. That obligation is the debt.

So the key feature of a debt is that the obligation to repay survives after the thing has been received and used.

In financial contexts, debt rarely stays the same size. When you borrow money, the lender typically charges you extra for the privilege of using their money — this extra charge is called interest.

So if you borrow ₹10,000 at 10% interest per year, after one year your debt is not ₹10,000 anymore — it's ₹11,000 (if you haven't paid anything back). The longer you take to repay, the larger the total debt can become.

This is why people say debt can "grow" or "accumulate."

"To be in debt" — means you currently owe money (or something else) to someone. It describes your ongoing situation.

"After buying a car on loan, she was in debt for three years."

"To get into debt" — means to enter a situation where you owe someone, usually by borrowing.

"He got into debt after losing his job and using credit cards to survive."

"To get out of debt" — means to fully repay what you owe, so you no longer owe anything.

"It took her five years, but she finally got out of debt."

"To repay a debt" / "to pay off a debt" — means to return what you owe, clearing the obligation.

"He worked overtime every week to repay his debt to the bank."

"To run up a debt" — means to accumulate a large debt gradually, often carelessly.

"She ran up a huge debt by shopping on credit without a plan to repay."

"To owe a debt" — the verb phrase simply states the relationship: you are the debtor, and this is what you owe.

"He owes a debt of ₹2 lakh to his uncle."
Debt in a Broader, Non-Financial Sense

Debt is not only about money. It is used in everyday life to describe any situation where you feel obligated to someone because of what they did for you.

"A debt of gratitude" — when someone does something very kind or important for you, you feel a deep sense of thankfulness and a desire to repay them — not with money, but with kindness, loyalty, or help in the future. This feeling is called a debt of gratitude.

"She feels a debt of gratitude to her mentor, who helped her get her first job."

"I owe you a debt" — said to someone who helped you greatly, acknowledging that you feel obligated to return the kindness someday.

In this non-financial sense, a debt is a moral or emotional obligation — an inner sense that you must do something for someone because they did something meaningful for you.
Debt as a Concept at Larger Scales

Debt doesn't just exist between individuals. It exists at every level of human life:

  • Personal debt — a person borrowing money from a bank or another person.
  • Business debt — a company that has borrowed money to operate or grow.
  • National debt (also called public debt) — the total amount of money a country's government owes to lenders (citizens, other countries, international institutions). Governments borrow by issuing bonds or taking loans, and the total unpaid amount is the national debt.

In all cases, the same logic applies: something was received → something is still owed → until it is repaid, the debt exists.
The Moral Weight of the Word

In everyday speech, "debt" carries a sense of weight and responsibility. Being in debt is generally seen as a burden — something you want to resolve. There's an implicit social and moral pressure to honour your debts, because someone trusted you enough to give you something before you gave them anything in return. Breaking that trust — by refusing to repay — is widely considered dishonest and irresponsible.

This is why the word "debt" is used in moral and emotional contexts too — it captures that sense of an unpaid obligation that you are expected to fulfil.

AspectExplanation

Debt is an unfulfilled obligation. You received something — money, help, kindness — and the equivalent has not yet been returned. The debt is the gap between what you received and what you've given back. It ends when that gap is closed — when you repay, return the favour, or fulfil the obligation in full. Until then, the debt stands.
3956:
To debunk something means to prove that a widely believed claim, story, or idea is false, misleading, or exaggerated — and to show this clearly, using facts, evidence, or reasoning, so that people can see it for what it really is.

Think of it this way: imagine a shiny bubble floating in the air. Everyone around you believes the bubble is magical. You then prove, using science, that it's just soap and air. You have just debunked the idea that the bubble is magical. You popped the illusion.
What Makes "Debunk" Different From Simply Saying "Prove Wrong"?

This is important, because "debunk" is not just a fancy synonym for "prove something is wrong." It carries a very specific meaning with built-in conditions:

The thing being debunked must have been believed or accepted by people — it must have had some level of credibility or popularity. You cannot debunk something nobody ever believed in the first place.

Debunking involves actively and deliberately showing a false thing to be false. It is not accidental. Someone makes an effort to investigate and expose it.

Debunking almost always relies on evidence or reasoning — not personal opinion.

There is also a communicative element — debunking is usually done so that others can see and understand that the claim is false. It serves a public purpose.

So debunking is about removing false credibility that something has earned among people.
What Kinds of Things Can Be Debunked?

The word feels most natural when paired with things like:

Myths — widely held false beliefs. "Scientists debunked the myth that humans only use 10% of their brains." (We actually use virtually all of it.)

Conspiracy theories — dramatic, unproven claims about hidden plots. "Researchers debunked the theory that the moon landing was faked."

Misconceptions — innocent but incorrect beliefs. "The article debunked several common misconceptions about nutrition."

Rumors — unverified stories spreading among people. "The journalist debunked the rumor by tracing it to its source and finding no evidence."

Pseudoscience — false ideas dressed up to look scientific. "The doctor debunked the claim that the vaccine causes autism."

Urban legends — popular, dramatic stories passed around for years that turn out to be untrue.

Notice the pattern: in every case, the false idea has some degree of public belief behind it. That is what makes debunking meaningful.
How It Works in a Sentence

Debunk is an action verb — someone does it. The person or group doing the debunking is the subject, and the false claim is the object.

"She debunked the theory." / "Scientists debunked the myth." / "The documentary debunks several popular legends."

It also works in the passive voice, where the focus shifts to the false belief itself:

"That theory has been debunked." / "The myth was thoroughly debunked by researchers."

When something has been "thoroughly debunked" or "completely debunked," it means the evidence against it is so strong and clear that there is no reasonable room left for doubt.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

"Debunk" carries a confident, assertive tone. When you say someone debunked something, you are saying they didn't merely question it — they demolished its credibility. It has a slightly forceful, authoritative feel.

It also often carries a sense of intellectual satisfaction — like catching a widely spread lie in public, or revealing a trick that fooled many people for years. This is why the word is especially popular in journalism, science communication, and fact-checking. It feels decisive.

Debunked — used as a past tense verb or adjective to describe something already proven false.
"He debunked the myth last year." / "That is a thoroughly debunked claim."

Debunking — the act or ongoing process of proving something false (can be a noun or a present participle).
"She spent years debunking pseudoscience." / "The debunking of this legend took decades."

Debunker — a person who regularly or professionally exposes false claims.
"He is a well-known debunker of conspiracy theories."

Do not confuse debunk with disprove. They are close, but meaningfully different:

Disprove simply means to show something is not true. It is neutral and broad — it can apply to any incorrect claim, big or small.

Debunk specifically means to expose and dismantle a popular or widely believed false claim — one that had real public credibility before someone tore it down.

You disprove a wrong calculation. You debunk a myth. The difference is in scale and context.

Also, avoid using "debunk" for small, personal corrections. If your friend thinks it is Tuesday when it is actually Wednesday, you do not "debunk" them — you simply correct them. Debunking is reserved for widely held false ideas, not everyday individual mistakes. The moment you say something is "debunked," you are implying it had a significant enough following to be worth a deliberate, evidence-based takedown.
3957:
A debut is the first time a person, thing, or group appears publicly — especially in a particular role, field, or capacity — in a way that is noticed, received, or witnessed by others.

The single most important idea packed into this word: a first, public, significant appearance.

Not every "first time" qualifies as a debut. If you sing a song alone in your room for the first time, that is not a debut. But if you step onto a stage and sing in front of an audience for the first time — that is a debut.

The word "debut" almost always involves an audience — real people watching, or the public in some form receiving it. The debut is the moment you (or something) are introduced to the world, or to a particular world.
It Is Always the First — and Only Once

A debut can only happen once in any given context. After that, every subsequent appearance is just another appearance.

  • A singer can make their debut on a big stage once. After that, they have performed there before.
  • A product can debut at a launch event once. The next year, it is no longer new.

This is what gives the word its weight: a debut is unrepeatable. It is a one-time gateway from "never done this publicly before" to "has now done this publicly."
Who or What Can Have a Debut

Almost anything that makes a first public appearance can have a debut:

People:

  • An actor stepping into a film for the first time has a film debut.
  • A cricket player appearing in an international match for the first time has their international debut.
  • A musician performing on a major stage for the first time makes their stage debut.

Creative works:

  • A novel appearing in bookstores for the first time makes its debut.
  • A TV show airing its first episode makes its debut on television.
  • A song entering a music chart for the first time makes its chart debut.

Products and companies:

  • A new car shown to the public for the first time at an auto expo makes its debut.
  • A company entering the stock market for the first time (an IPO) makes its market debut.

Teams and organizations:

  • A newly formed sports team playing its first official match makes its debut in the league.

A debut is rarely treated as an ordinary moment. It usually carries:

  • Anticipation — people are waiting and watching to see how it goes.
  • Significance — it marks a beginning, a crossing of a threshold.
  • Judgment — the world is forming its first impression, which often sticks.
  • Pressure (for people) — because you only get one first impression.

This is why you often hear phrases like "a stunning debut", "a disappointing debut", or "a highly anticipated debut" — people pay close attention to debuts.
Common Phrases Using "Debut" as a Noun

• "make one's debut" — to appear publicly for the first time in a role.
    "She made her debut as a director with this film."
  • "debut on [something]" — first appearance on a stage, chart, platform, etc.
    "The song's debut on the charts was at number three."
  • "a debut performance" — the very first performance someone gives in a role.
    "His debut performance as Hamlet received standing ovations."
  • "a debut album" — the first album an artist releases publicly.
    "Her debut album sold a million copies in the first week."

A debut is not just about being new — it is about being introduced. Something debuts when it steps forward and presents itself to a world that has not seen it in that role before. There is an implicit sense of: "Here I am, for the first time, in this capacity — take notice."

This is why the word carries more weight than simply saying "the first time." Saying "his debut in cricket" communicates not just that it was his first match, but that it was a meaningful, public crossing into a new arena.

A debut is the first time a person, creative work, product, or group appears publicly in a particular role or field — a moment that can only happen once, that others witness, and that carries the significance of a beginning.
3958:
A debutante is a young woman, usually from a wealthy or upper-class family, who is formally and publicly introduced to "society" for the very first time at a special event — most commonly a grand ball or ceremony. This event is called her debut.

Think of it like an official announcement to the world that says: "This young woman has grown up, and she is now entering adult social life."

The word "society" here doesn't just mean people in general. It refers to a specific group — the upper class, the elite, the wealthy and powerful circles of a community or country. Being introduced to this society meant you were now recognized as a full member of it. You had a seat at the table, so to speak.
What a Debutante Event Looks Like

The debut event (often called a debutante ball or coming-out ball) is typically a very formal, elegant affair. Here is what it usually involves:

  • The young woman wears a white or light-colored formal gown. White was traditionally chosen to symbolize purity and innocence.
  • She is accompanied by a male escort — sometimes a relative, sometimes a chosen companion — who presents her.
  • She is formally introduced by name to the guests in attendance.
  • She may curtsy (a formal bow done by women, bending the knees gracefully) before the guests or before a figure of authority.
  • There is dancing, socializing, and celebration.

The whole event is designed to be graceful, refined, and memorable. It is a performance of elegance and status.

A debutante is typically:

  • Young — usually between 16 and 21 years old, most commonly around 17 or 18.
  • From a wealthy or prominent family — historically, this was almost exclusively for the aristocracy (nobility) or the very wealthy upper class.
  • Female — the tradition is specific to young women, though the related male term is "debutant."

Understanding why this tradition existed makes the word much clearer.

In earlier centuries — particularly in Europe and America — a young woman's entry into adult society had a very specific, practical purpose: it signaled that she was now old enough and eligible to be married. The debutante ball was, in many ways, a formal announcement to eligible bachelors (and their families) that this particular young woman was now "available" as a potential wife.

It was also about social gatekeeping — only certain families had the privilege and prestige to have their daughters formally "come out" into elite society. It was a mark of status, not just for the girl, but for her entire family.

So the debutante tradition was deeply tied to three things: age, marriage, and class.

Over time — especially through the 20th and 21st centuries — the tradition has shifted in meaning:

  • The marriage-market aspect has largely faded. Today, most people don't see a debutante ball as advertising a girl for marriage.
  • It is now more commonly seen as a rite of passage — a celebration of a young woman transitioning into adulthood.
  • Many modern debutante events are tied to charity fundraising, where the ball raises money for a good cause while also serving as the social event.
  • The tradition has spread and adapted across many cultures, sometimes with unique local flavor. In the Philippines, for example, a girl's 18th birthday is celebrated as her "debut" — a lavish party marking her entry into womanhood. In Latin American communities, a similar tradition exists for 15-year-olds and is called a Quinceañera.

Words carry feelings and associations beyond their bare definition, and "debutante" is no different.

When people use this word, it often carries these underlying ideas:

  • Wealth and privilege — a debutante is assumed to come from money and a prominent family.
  • Refinement and elegance — she is polished, well-dressed, and well-mannered.
  • Formality and tradition — the whole concept is rooted in old, formal social customs.
  • Sometimes, a slightly old-fashioned or even superficial feeling — because some people view the tradition as outdated or as a display of snobbery.

So depending on the context, calling someone a debutante can sound admiring (she is refined and high-class) or gently mocking (she is overly privileged and sheltered).
One Helpful Image to Lock It In

Imagine a grand ballroom filled with chandelier light and formally dressed guests. A young woman in a white gown walks in, is announced by name, curtsies gracefully, and is applauded. Everyone now knows her as an official, recognized member of elite society. That young woman is the debutante.

A debutante is a young upper-class woman who is being formally introduced to society for the first time, usually at a grand ball. The word captures the intersection of youth, wealth, formality, and social status. Historically tied to marriage eligibility, the tradition today is more about celebrating adulthood and maintaining cultural customs among elite or prominent families.
3959:
Decadence is the state of falling into excessive self-indulgence, luxury, and pleasure-seeking — especially when this represents a decline from a previously higher standard of discipline, morality, or strength.

The word carries two ideas braided together: decline (falling away from something better) and indulgence (surrendering to pleasure, comfort, and excess). These two aren't just sitting side by side — in decadence, the indulgence is the decline, or at least causes it.

Imagine a person who was once disciplined, hardworking, and principled. Slowly, they start sleeping late, spending money recklessly, eating and drinking to excess, skipping their responsibilities, and caring only about their own comfort and entertainment. They've stopped striving for anything meaningful. That slow drift — away from discipline and toward lazy, self-centered pleasure-seeking — captures the spirit of decadence.

Now scale that up to an entire society. When a whole civilization moves in that direction — becoming obsessed with luxury, spectacle, and pleasure while neglecting its values and moral seriousness — historians call that decadence too. The most famous example people reach for is the late Roman Empire, which is often described as having sunk into decadence: lavish banquets, brutal entertainment, corruption, and self-indulgence, while the discipline and civic virtue that had built Rome crumbled away.
What Makes It Different from Simply "Enjoying Yourself"

This is an important distinction. Decadence is not just about enjoying nice things. Everyone enjoys comfort and pleasure — that is normal and human. Decadence describes what happens when the pursuit of pleasure becomes so excessive that it erodes something important: your values, your discipline, your responsibilities, or society's moral health. The key element is that something of real value is being lost or sacrificed in the process. Decadence has a rotten core beneath its luxurious surface.

Decadence almost always carries a tone of criticism or disapproval, even when it is not stated directly. When someone says a society has fallen into decadence, they are not simply describing what people are doing — they are implying that something has gone wrong. There is always an invisible comparison to a better past, a golden age of strength or virtue from which the present has fallen. Decadence implies corruption — not of the dishonest, criminal kind necessarily, but a softer, more insidious corruption where people have become too comfortable, too self-absorbed, and too pleasure-focused to care about what truly matters.
The Spectrum: From Heavy to Light

In practice, people use "decadence" across a spectrum of seriousness, and you'll encounter all of these in real life.

At the most serious end, it describes the deep moral and cultural decline of a civilization. "The decadence of the Roman Empire" or "a society in decadence" — here the word carries its full weight of moral judgment and historical gravity.

In the middle, it describes a lifestyle or period in a person's life marked by excessive self-indulgence and moral looseness. "Years of decadence had left him hollow and directionless" — here it's personal and mildly critical.

At the lightest end, and this is common in modern everyday speech, decadence is used almost admiringly to describe something luxuriously, sinfully rich — especially food. A chocolate cake layered with cream and ganache might be called "a moment of pure decadence." Here, the moral criticism has almost entirely fallen away, and the word simply means gloriously, over-the-top indulgent. This lighter use keeps the idea of excess but strips away the darker undertone.

So the word can be used seriously or playfully, harshly or warmly, depending on context. You need to read the surrounding sentence to know which shade is meant.

There is also a specific cultural and artistic meaning worth knowing. In the late 19th century, a movement emerged — particularly in French and English literature — called the Decadent Movement. Writers and artists in this movement deliberately embraced decadence as a philosophy and an aesthetic. They celebrated sensory pleasure, beauty, artifice, and moral unconventionality, and they rejected what they saw as the dull, moralistic values of mainstream society. The Irish writer Oscar Wilde is probably the most famous figure associated with this tradition. So when you read about "the decadence of fin-de-siècle literature," it refers to this specific artistic philosophy, not necessarily a criticism.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Hedonism is the philosophy of pursuing pleasure as life's main goal. Decadence is what hedonism looks like when it has truly taken over and begun to cause damage — it is hedonism with consequences.

Debauchery is more specifically about wild, immoral behavior involving excessive drinking, sex, and revelry. It is louder and more scandalous. Decadence is broader and can be quieter — a slow softening rather than an outright scandal.

Dissipation is very close to decadence and describes wasting one's energy, health, or resources through self-indulgent living. Decadence tends to be used on a larger cultural or moral scale; dissipation often feels more personal.

Corruption is broader and can mean many things including dishonesty and crime. Decadence is specifically about pleasure-seeking and moral softening, not dishonesty.

"The historian argued that it was not military defeat but internal decadence that destroyed the empire."

"After years of decadence — the parties, the excess, the utter disregard for discipline — he found himself with nothing to show for his thirties."

"She allowed herself one evening of pure decadence: room service, a long bath, and three episodes of her favourite show."

"The novel is a portrait of Parisian decadence at the turn of the century."

In short: Decadence is the condition of having fallen — or of falling — into excessive, self-indulgent pleasure and luxury, in a way that reflects or causes a decline in moral seriousness, discipline, or values. It can describe a civilization, a period in someone's life, an artistic movement, or, more lightly, simply something indulgently, richly luxurious. The more serious the context, the stronger its note of criticism and moral weight.
